data.content_ref: inline:The target's central mechanism relies on the analogy that preferring corroborated theories is a constitutive norm 'similar to check your king in chess.' This analogy is self-undermining. Constitutive rules of games are arbitrary conventions: they define the activity but have no justification outside the activity itself—there is no reason chess requires checking the king rather than some other rule. If the rule 'prefer the better-corroborated theory' is constitutive in exactly this sense, then it is an arbitrary convention with no rational defense: one could with equal constitutive legitimacy adopt 'prefer the theory of the eldest scientist.' The only thing that distinguishes the corroboration rule as worth adopting over arbitrary alternatives is that it tracks truth or reliability—which is an epistemic justification that, per Popper's problem, must not smuggle in induction. Thus the chess analogy either makes the rule arbitrary (so not 'rationally defensible,' merely conventional) or forces an appeal to truth-conduciveness (reintroducing the very inductive assumption the target sought to avoid). The target's own mechanistic framing collapses its claim of defensibility.
